description: How can a country dominate the world without going to war? By simply making others want to be like him.

hero.hook: Seduce the world rather than conquer it: the secret of American power.

blocks.text: How can a country dominate the world without going to war? By simply making others want to be like him. This is the idea behind **soft power**, or “soft power,” a concept that has changed the way we understand relations between countries.
The United States is the most studied example. But this influence through seduction, as powerful as it is, today shows signs of fragility.

In 1990, in his book *Bound to Lead*, the American political scientist **Joseph Nye** invented a new word: **soft power**. He opposes it to **hard power**, hard power, which brings together the army and economic sanctions. Soft power is based on attraction: convincing rather than forcing. According to Nye, this influence is based on three pillars: **culture**, when it pleases other peoples, **political values** like democracy, provided they are truly applied at home, and **foreign policy**, legitimate if it is perceived as fair by the rest of the world.

Hollywood produces around 700 films per year, compared to more than 1,800 for Bollywood in India. However, American films capture around 70% of global cinema revenues: proof that influence depends less on quantity than on control of distribution networks.
This ability to make others adhere without forcing them recalls an older idea, the : to dominate not by force, but by imposing one's ideas as evidence shared by all. **[[Cultural hegemony]]**

Since the end of World War I, the United States has built an unparalleled cultural empire. American cinema exports a way of life, consumption habits, and the English language. Music, from jazz to hip-hop, extends this influence, as do the 's elite universities, which train many of the world's leaders. **[[Ivy League]]**

blocks.caption: For a century, Hollywood, music and American universities have exported a way of life admired around the world.

blocks.text: In the 21st century, this power has shifted to digital. American tech giants control the search algorithms and social networks used by billions of people, giving the United States a unique ability to structure global public debate.

Soft power is a fragile resource: it depends entirely on credibility. In 2003, the invasion of Iraq, carried out without the agreement of the **UN** and justified by evidence of weapons which turned out to be false, lastingly damaged the image of the United States, now perceived by some as an imperialist power.

Other internal crises have had the same effect: the financial crisis of 2008 discredited the American economic model, and the assault on the Capitol in January 2021 weakened the image of the United States as a model of stable democracy. When a country no longer lives according to its values, its influence collapses.

At the same time, a new form of influence emerged: . The European Union sets such strict rules on its own market, on data protection or the environment, that large companies prefer to apply them everywhere in the world rather than adapting them country by country. The influence then no longer comes only through dreams, but through the law. **[[“Brussels Effect”]]**

sections.title: The decline of a contested model

blocks.text: The United States is no longer alone in the field of seduction. China is investing in cultural institutes and huge infrastructure projects across Asia and Africa, offering an alternative development model that is attracting many countries in the South.

Other countries rely on more targeted soft power. Japan seduces with its mangas and its gastronomy, while South Korea has built its own cultural wave, the  (music, series, cinema), which is conquering a global audience. Cultural attractiveness is no longer reserved for the West. **[[Hallyu]]**

There is an annual ranking, the Soft Power 30, which measures the attractiveness of countries. The United States held first place for a long time, before being overtaken by France or Germany during the presidency of Donald Trump, proof of the direct link between foreign policy and the image of a country.

American soft power, based on cinema, universities and digital technology, remains the most structuring force of influence on globalization. But it is increasingly competing with new models, those of China, South Korea or even the European Union.
